Fundamental Cosmic Anisotropy and its Ramifications II Perturbations in Bianchi spacetimes, and fixed in the Newtonian gauge Preprint: APS/123-QED
Robbert W. Scholtens, Marcello Seri, Holger Waalkens, Rien van de Weygaert

Abstract
The standard cosmological model is challenged by an ever-growing collection of observations, which invites (and stimulates) inquiry into possible additions and/or alterations. One such alteration comes from letting cosmic isotropy—as demanded by the cosmological principle—go, whilst maintaining only homogeneity. This study concerns Bianchi models, a class of anisotropic, homogeneous spacetimes, and in particular their perturbations. Knowledge of their properties under perturbations (such as allowed wavemodes) aids in understanding cosmological signatures of such universes, e.g. CMBs, and thus allows for comparsion to observation and the theory of the standard model. This study develops linear perturbation theory of general Bianchi models, by working in a frame such that metric components depend solely on (cosmic) time. Perturbation equations in the Newtonian gauge, but for arbitrary metric, are derived for energy density ρ \rho , (relativistic) pressure p p , momentum density 𝒒 \bm{q} , and anisotropic stress 𝝅 \bm{\pi} , for the case of scalar and pure tensor perturbations. For the former, the equations for density and pressure are combined to yield the equivalent of the Mukhanov-Sasaki equation for Bianchi models. For a specific choice of metric and fluid flow 𝒖 \bm{u} , the Friedmann equations for Bianchi models are also formulated, as this knowledge is necessary to fully formulate the perturbation equations. Finally, the obtained results are applied to the formulations of density contrasts in an Einstein-de Sitter universe and a Bianchi I universe.



I
Introduction

Modern cosmology is based on the Cosmological Principle, stating that at the largest scales, the universe is spatially homogeneous and isotropic
(
32
, §3)
,
35
, which heuristically means that every location in space is equivalent, as well as every spatial direction. From this, together with the Weyl principle
(
31
, §3.4)
and Einstein’s general relativity, one can then derive the
Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker
(FLRW) model—the backbone of the “standard model of cosmology,”
\Lambda
CDM. This model allows us to explain observations with great success, an example being given by the CMB power spectrum as measured by the
Planck
mission
41
.

Recently, though, certain challenges to this standard model have been emerging. These include an observed potential anisotropy in the Hubble parameter
4
;
25
;
5
, anisotropy in the cosmic acceleration
7
;
43
, anisotropies in quasar distributions
49
;
53
and supernovae
45
;
8
, and local bulk flows
56
. Peebles also gives an overview of “anomalies” not (yet) resolved by
\Lambda
CDM in
36
;
35
. There is also the excellent recent review by Kumar Aluri et al. on compatibility of the cosmological principle with observations
19
. As the sources cited above indicate, it may be that isotropy as postulated by the cosmological principle deserves some reconsideration, while still maintaining cosmic homogeneity—enter, thus, the homogeneous,
anisotropic
cosmologies. Loosely speaking, these are cosmologies in which every spatial location is still equivalent, but spatial directions are no longer all equivalent; one could also say, there is (at least one)
preferred
direction in space. These models can further be subdivided into types with varying degrees of rotational symmetry
(
13
, §5.2)
.

In continuance of our previous work
48
, our primary interest is in the
Bianchi
models, those generally without any additional symmetry other than homogeneity. Such models have been studied ever since their introduction in the 1960s
12
;
10
;
24
;
9
;
20
—see also
14
for a brief overview.

Our interests lay with
perturbations
of such universes. Physically, cosmological perturbations manifest themselves as structures in the universe, such as the the CMB or the cosmic web, and observations of these structures forms the empirical basis for cosmological models. Understanding perturbations of Bianchi models, thus, leads to further understanding of the signatures of anisotropy. The presence of these signatures—or lack thereof—can then form a probe for assessing the validity of the Cosmological Principle, and to which extent (for instance, homogeneity scales).

In the FLRW model, this is a well-studied and well-understood field of inquiry—see for instance Peebles’ seminal textbook
The Large-Scale Structure of the Universe

33
. The study of perturbations of Bianchi models has mostly revolved around perturbations of the so-called Bianchi I model, which for distinct functions
a(t)
,
b(t)
, and
c(t)
, has a metric expressible as

\differential{s}^{2}=-\differential{t}^{2}+a^{2}(\differential{x})^{2}+b^{2}(\differential{y})^{2}+c^{2}(\differential{z})^{2};

(I.1)

see e.g.
23
;
21
;
17
;
37
. These models are still quite tractable analytically, and allow some of the same analysis techniques as for FLRW. Another model of particular interest is Bianchi VII
2
;
40
;
42
. Analyses of non-Bianchi I models usually assume some manner of closeness to FLRW, grounded in the current observations and closeness to isotropy, or single scale factor (despite, like above, multiple being allowed), to reduce complexity.

In this paper, we study perturbations of Bianchi spacetimes—not a priori restricted to a specific type—by working in an adapted frame (or tetrad) for our spacetime, and performing the analysis as is traditionally carried out for FLRW universes. Such frames have been considered at length in the literature
50
;
18
, and provide a popular method of studying Bianchi spacetimes. In such a frame, one may then derive objects of interest such as the kinematical quantities and the Friedmann equations. More specifically, the frame we choose is such that

1.

the spacetime metric for our Bianchi model has metric components
dependent solely on cosmic time
t
;
and

2.

the constituent vector fields form a Lie algebra.

That this can be done is elaborated on, for instance, in our previous work
48
. With these two properties, the Einstein field equations reduce from partial to ordinary differential equations, improving solvability. The price that is being paid is a more complicated interpretation of the results, and that we need to take into account effects due to, in general, non-coordinate frame we are using. Nevertheless, in said frame we can then still proceed with a perturbation analysis, carried out in the usual fashion.

In §

III

\bm{u}

|\bm{u}|^{2}=-1

II
Preliminaries

II.1
Homogeneous geometries

Any spacetime metric
\bm{g}
that is spatially homogeneous has---by definition---three spacelike Killing vector fields (KVFs) that at each event in spacetime are independent of each other. Under the assumption of simple transitivity,
1
1

1

That is, that when following the flow of one KVF, the flow of another KVF will not be intersected.
these generates a spacelike hypersurface in spacetime
(
44
, §6.3)
. Then, congruent with the assumption of global hyperbolicity, spacetime can
globally
be split as
\Sigma^{3}\times\mathbb{R}
, i.e. “
\text{spacetime}=\text{space}\times\text{time}
,” or foliated with copies of that spacelike hypersurface. Note that this decomposition is purely
topological;
for instance the precise embeddings of the
\mathbb{R}
and
\Sigma^{3}
into spacetime are not determined from this observation.

do not generally allow this coordinate-like interpretation. A frame in which not all of the structure constants vanish is thus called
non-coordinated.
Physically, this means that the directions may be “non-constant,” by which we mean that their very definition—the vector field
\mathchoice{\bm{X}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\bm{X}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\bm{X}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\bm{X}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}
—may vary from place to place. But, by construction they are independent of time, so however they change, there is no temporal dependence.

The above formulation (
II.1
) allows us to write any spatially homogeneous metric into a “separated form,” wherein the spatial information is absorbed into the basis of 1-forms, and the temporal information into the actual components of the metric. Clearly, we should prefer to work in this separated form over any other presented form of a spatially homogeneous metric: since the metric components depend only on time, this will reduce the Einstein equations from partial to ordinary differential equations—a huge simplification. The cost we pay is geometric non-triviality under the hood.

We assume from now on that
any frame is not necessarily coordinated,
but that it is has the properties outlined above. That is, that the frame for spacetime

Note that coordinate frames also satisfy this definition, in which case the structure constants vanish identically (as the frame vector fields are partial derivatives of the coordinates, which commute).

One non-triviality comes from having to reconsider the Levi-Civita connection. On any (pseudo-)Riemannian manifold, it is the unique connection that is both compatible with metric and torsion-free. Its definition in a local frame is given by
(
44
, §2.5)

. This reduces the known formula for the Christoffel symbols in the case the frame is coordinate. Note that the structure constants of our frame are introduced as proportional to the metric, instead of a derivative, and also a constant term is added. This destroys the symmetry in the lower two indices of the Levi-Civita connection; or, the Levi-Civita connection is symmetric if and only if all structure constants vanish, i.e. that our frame is coordinated.

II.2
The 1+3 decomposition

Not only is a cosmological model we choose to study dependent on its metric, but also on the inherent movement of so-called “fundamental particles”: large-scale objects such as galaxy clusters which are assumed to move under gravity alone. In this way, the cosmos can be seen as a “fluid” with these fundamental particles as the “molecules” that make it up. (A more refined version of this statement is known as Weyl’s postulate
(
31
, §3.5.1)
.) The 4-velocity of this fluid flow mathematically comes in the form of a vector field on spacetime, and is denoted by
\bm{u}
. We can also view
\bm{u}
as a family of observers, in which case its flow can be seen as an observer’s world line with tangent vector
\bm{u}
along it
(
11
, §4.2)
.

The choice of fluid flow, being related to an observer’s worldline, influences among others the notion of energy density
\rho
and pressure
p
appearing in the Friedmann equations of the cosmological model. This can be seen, for instance, by examining the energy-momentum tensor for a perfect fluid,

\mathchoice{T^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{T^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{T^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{T^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}=(\rho+p)\,\mathchoice{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}\mathchoice{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}+p\,\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\ma (II.7)

Hence, different choices of
\bm{u}
will eventually lead to different values for
\rho
and
p
, when writing down the Friedmann equations.

Though in principle any choice of
\bm{u}
can be made from a mathematical point of view, a physical requirement is that the fluid flow is timelike, i.e. that
\mathchoice{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}<0
at every event—if it were not, it could not be tangent to observers’ worldlines. In fact, we shall normalize the fluid flow (which is a matter of reparametrization), so that we make the common assumption that at every event,
\mathchoice{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{u^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}=-1
.

Another common assumption is the one of geodesic fluid flow, i.e. fluid flows wherein the condition
\mathchoice{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}:=\mathchoice{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{u^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{;\alpha}}}}{u^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{;\alpha}}}}{u^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{;\alpha}}}}{u^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{;\alpha}}}}\equiv 0
. This corresponds to observers along the fluid flow to be in constant free fall, i.e. free movement along geodesics in spacetime. However, in this work we elect
not
to make this assumption, and instead carry
\mathchoice{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
through the calculations. If at a later stage we wish to consider geodesic fluid flows instead, we may then at that moment set
\mathchoice{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\equiv 0
.

In the field of cosmology, often the particular choice of fluid flow is made as
\mathchoice{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\mathchoice{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}=(1,0,0,0)
, for
\mathchoice{x^{{{0}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{0}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{0}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{0}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=t
the cosmic time. This corresponds to the cosmic fluid being at rest on the largest scales. The rationale is that for the timelike object with 4-velocity
\bm{u}
, a frame featuring
\bm{u}
as one of the basis vector fields can be defined; in that frame, then, the object is spatially stationary. Thus, the object only has motion in the timelike direction, which can subsequently be normalized (e.g. corresponding to a choice of metric coefficient
\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}{0}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}{0}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}{0}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}{0}}}}
). This also synergizes well with the cosmological principle, which through isotropy forbids any preferred spatial directions. If we did choose a frame in which
\bm{u}
corresponded to motion through space, the projection of
\bm{u}
onto space could be argued to be a preferred spatial direction, contradicting isotropy. Since in our studies we are interested especially in letting go of the spatial isotropy assumption, we do
not
assume that
\mathchoice{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\propto\mathchoice{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}
and only assume normalization.

Now that we have established that there is a preferred timelike direction at every event, being the fluid flow
\bm{u}
, it makes intuitive and mathematical sense to split tensorial quantities according to their components along and perpendicular to this fluid flow. This is what we shall develop for the rest of this section.

II.2.1
Decomposing tensors

In order to study the components of a tensor along and perpendicular to the fluid flow
\bm{u}
, we need an operator that facilitates this splitting. For this we introduce the
projection operator

\bm{h}
, as

\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}:=\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\make (II.8)

which has the properties that

\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[13.3994pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[13.3994pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[8.09523pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.78227pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{[\mu\nu]}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[13.3994pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[13.3994pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[8.09523pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.78227pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{[\mu\nu]}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[13.3994pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[13.3994pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[8.09523pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.78227pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{[\mu\nu]}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[13.3994pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[13.3994pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[8.09523pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.78227pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{[\mu\nu]}}}}=0,\quad\mathchoice{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}=0,\mbox{\quad and\quad}\mathchoice{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}\mathchoice{h^{{{\alpha}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{h^{{{\alpha}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{h^{{{\alpha}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{h^{{{\alpha}}}_{{{\nu}}}}=\mathchoice{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{h^{{{\mu}}}_{{{\nu}}}}

(II.9)

so that indeed
\bm{h}
projects a vector onto a subspace perpendicular to
\bm{u}
in the tangent space above each event in spacetime. In fact, since
\bm{h}
can be viewed as the pullback of
\bm{g}
under the embedding of this subspace into spacetime
(
11
, §2.9)
, it follows that
\bm{h}
projects vectors onto a hypersurface. Note that
\bm{h}
is the first fundamental form of the hypersurface. The projection tensor
\bm{h}
can be used as the metric on this hypersurface, and, since the sole timelike direction has been projected away, this metric is Riemannian.

Let us now do some projections. Assume that we wish to project the symmetric 2-tensor

(II.14)

II.2.2
The wave operator and its projection(s)

We shall also be interested in the projection properties of derivatives and differential operators. Naturally, these will tell us about the projected changes in quantities of interest. Given standard theory, the
wave operator
or
d’Alembertian
is defined by the formula

(II.15)

for scalar functions
f
, and analogously for tensors. It is so called since in the Minkowski metric, the kernel of
\square
consists of precisely those functions which satisfy the Euclidean wave equation. It shall turn out that we want to consider a decomposition of this operator utilizing the fluid flow that we have defined, thereby obtaining an operator “along” the fluid flow, and an operator for the perpendicular hypersurfaces. The most straightforward way to carry this out is by decomposing the metric
\bm{g}
in the above definition of the wave operator:

(II.16)

(Here and from now on, the dot operator on any tensor indicates differentiation along the fluid flow.) Since the hypersurface onto which we project with
\bm{h}
is spatial (any tangent vector to it is spacelike), we
could
conclude that

is the Laplace-Beltrami operator (or Laplacian) for the hypersurface.

This would go contrary to the literature, though. The definition of the Laplacian of a scalar function
f
is
\triangle f:=\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{grad}f)

(
38
, §2.1)
. If one thus wants to consider the Laplacian restricted to a submanifold (such as our perpendicular hypersurface is, through the embedding into spacetime), the divergence and gradient should be taken on the hypersurface. That is, by using a projected covariant derivative:
\mathchoice{D^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{D^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{D^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{D^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}f:=\mathchoice{h^{{{\alpha}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{h^{{{\alpha}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{h^{{{\alpha}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{h^{{{\alpha}}}_{{{\mu}}}}\,\mathchoice{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}f
for scalar functions
f
. For tensorial objects, the definition becomes slightly more complicated
(

, §4.4.2)

(II.20)

Physical interpretations of these quantities are discussed in e.g.
(
15
, §2.5)
. In summary, (i) the expansion scalar
\theta
quantifies the expansion/contraction of a fluid element as it travels along its worldline, (ii) the shear
\bm{\sigma}
describes the change in its shape normalized to constant volume, and (iii) the vorticity
\bm{\omega}
indicates its rotation.

This decomposition moreover paves the way for the Raychaudhuri equation. This couples the kinematical scalars, differentiated fluid flow, and the Ricci tensor contracted along the fluid direction. The traditional way to derive it is to contract the Ricci identity for the Riemann tensor (
II.6
): first contracting the Riemann tensor, and then contractin with another
\bm{u}
. The result is the following:

We shall first briefly discuss the mathematical context in which (cosmological) perturbation theory is placed, letting us define perturbations in a solid mathematical manner. Subsequently, we calculate and simplify the perturbations (to first order) in the (i) spacetime metric, (ii) energy-momentum tensor (EMT), and (iii) the Einstein tensor, for which we also use an instance of the Mathematica package
xPand

39
. We can then formulate the perturbed Einstein equations (
III.1
), which are then to be solved in the subsequent section where we fix the Newtonian gauge.

(III.4)

where
\mathcal{L}^{k}_{X}
is the Lie derivative w.r.t.
\bm{X}
, applied
k
times. Then we can make the definitions
\delta^{(k)}\!\!\left[\bm{\tau}\right]:=\left[\mathcal{L}^{k}_{\bm{X}}\bm{\tau}\right]_{\mathchoice{\hphantom{{}^{{{(0)}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.19443pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathcal{M}^{{\kern-10.63899pt{(0)}\kern 5.94453pt}}_{{\kern-20.47787pt\mathchoice{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.19443pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 5.94453pt}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{(0)}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.19443pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathcal{M}^{{\kern-10.63899pt{(0)}\kern 5.94453pt}}_{{\kern-20.47787pt\mathchoice{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.19443pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 5.94453pt}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{(0)}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.19443pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathcal{M}^{{\kern-6.62498pt{(0)}\kern 3.20833pt}}_{{\kern-13.65273pt\mathchoice{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.19443pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 3.20833pt}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{(0)}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.19443pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathcal{M}^{{\kern-5.70833pt{(0)}\kern 2.29167pt}}_{{\kern-12.73607pt\mathchoice{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.81955pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.19443pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 2.29167pt}}}}
to represent the
k
th order perturbation to
\bm{\tau}
, and we obtain the series

\alpha_{\epsilon}^{*}\bm{\tau}|_{{}^{(0)}\!\mathcal{M}}=\,^{(0)}\bm{\tau}+\epsilon\,\delta^{(1)}\!\!\left[\bm{\tau}\right]+\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon^{2}\,\delta^{(2)}\!\!\left[\bm{\tau}\right]+\order{\epsilon^3}

(III.5)

This expansion defines the mathematical context in which the perturbation to
\bm{\tau}
, an arbitrary tensor of interest, is defined. We now proceed with applying this expansion to the metric tensor, and subsequently the energy-momentum and Einstein tensors.

(III.7)

The dots indicate that in order to effect perfect equality, one would need to solve the infinitude of equations for all orders of
\epsilon
that follow. Truncating the solution to, for our purposes, first order implies that the relation of inverses holds only up to second order.

The zeroth order equation is satisfied by virtue of
\overline{\bm{g}}
being a background metric. The first order equation can be solved for either the
(0,2)
- or
(2,0)
-valence, first order perturbation in terms of the other. Since the metric with
(0,2)
-valence is more fundamental (reflecting its definition as acting on the tangent bundle), we shall solve the second relation in (
III.7
) for the upper index configuration in terms of the lower one:

(III.9)

From now on, we drop the overbar on the background metric, and assume that any appearance of the metric is the background one.

\bm{q}
is the momentum density vector, and
\bm{\pi}

.)

We also emphasize that once
\rho
and
p
are defined by means of an arbitrary frame, say
\mathbb{F}
, they are invariant under diffeomorphisms of
\mathbb{F}
. However, supposing that
\mathbb{F}
is non-coordinate, it will not be related to a coordinate frame, say
\mathbb{G}
, via diffeomorphism. Therefore, the expressions may change, and in particular, they may pick up dependencies that were not there to begin with—concretely, if
\rho
and
p
defined in
\mathbb{F}
depend only on cosmic time, they may also depend on space in
\mathbb{G}
. The reason is that these are
densities,
and the volumes against which they are defined are the ones stemming from the metric. Since the metric, when expressed in
\mathbb{G}
, will pick up dependence on space,
\rho
and
p
will too. Physically, the reasoning is that the “amount” of energy/momentum located near an event is equal for both frames, but the local volume is not. Thus, their densities, as found through the EMT, will not be either.

The continuity equation for this general, decomposed EMT (
III.10
) is

(III.14)

As in the previous subsection, we read this equation as an equality between
perturbations of components
of tensors. We should like to work with
components of perturbations,
however, for the perturbations are tensors and thus easier to handle mathematically. In order to go from the former to the latter, we make the definitions

(III.15)

Just as with the metric tensor above, these definitions linking perturbations of components to components of perturbations represent the original objects and their perturbations. For instance, the perturbation of the vector field
\bm{u}
,
\delta^{(1)}\!\bm{u}
, is once more a vector field, and so its natural index position is up. From another point of view: when speaking of the vector field
\bm{u}
,

(III.17)

We now wish to project this equation along and perpendicular to the fluid flow, as that will allow us to extract the perturbed components of interest. To do so efficiently, we also employ some identities between the perturbations that follow from perturbing known relations. For instance,

III.4
The Einstein tensor & Einstein equation

The variation in the Einstein tensor is trickier to find, since it involves covariant differentiation of quantities. By virtue of the metric being perturbed, the Christoffel symbols are also perturbed and hence covariant differentiation becomes more involved. Although an analytical approach is possible via the Palatini identity for the perturbations of the Ricci tensor
(
27
, §35.13)
, we instead utilize the Mathematica package
xPand

39
, based on
xAct
, in order to produce a “raw” first order perturbation to the Einstein tensor. We then massage the resulting expression, eventually ending up with the following perturbation equation:

(III.24d)

IV
Fixing the Newtonian gauge

Up to now, our treatment has been entirely general. That is to say, it holds for any metric, metric frame, and choice of perturbation. (We only fixed the conditions on the fluid flow 4-vector
\bm{u}
, see §
II.2
.) We shall now evaluate these equations for perturbations
fixed to the Newtonian gauge.
We do this for two reasons: firstly, this is closest to our desired application to CMB analysis and structure formation; and secondly, the metric theory of gauge transformations and invariance is complicated to such an extent that it would cloud any useful conclusions to be drawn from this approach. Much research on cosmological gauge theory, and with an eye towards application in homogeneous, anisotropic spacetimes, has been done, and can be found in e.g.
30
;
51
.

We first proceed with evaluating pure scalar perturbations in the Newtonian gauge. A thermodynamical argument then allows us to link the perturbations in the density and pressure, in order to give one equation that must be satisfied by the perturbation at all events. This will be the equivalent of the Mukhanov-Sasaki equation for our setting of homogeneous, anisotropic spacetimes. We then proceed with evaluating pure tensor mode perturbations, as such an analysis and understanding may prove useful for gravitational wave analyses in anisotropic spacetimes.

IV.1

(IV.2d)

(IV.3d)

Finally, we wish to combine the equations above, particularly (
IV.3a
) and (
IV.3b
), in order to arrive at an equation that parallels the “standard” equation for scalar perturbation theory—found e.g. in
(
11
, §10.2)
—as announced above. In order to keep as much generalization open as possible, we do not a priori assume an isentropic perturbation. The relation between pressure and density perturbations is thus given by
(
29
, §7.5)

\delta^{(1)}\!p=c_{s}^{2}\,\delta^{(1)}\!\rho+\tau\delta S,\quad\mbox{where}\quad c_{s}:=\sqrt{\left(\partialderivative{p}{\rho}\right)_{S}}\mbox{\quad and\quad}\tau:=\left(\partialderivative{p}{S}\right)_{\rho},

(IV.4)

where
\delta S
represents the change in entropy due to the perturbation. In the above,
c_{s}
has the interpretation of the speed of sound in the medium, and
\tau
of a temperature in the therodynamic sense. Populating this relation (
IV.4
) with (
IV.3a
) and (
IV.3b
) and shuffling some terms around, we find the relation

\begin{split}3\kappa\tau\,\delta S&=6\ddot{\psi}-6c_{s}^{2}\lozenge\psi+2\lozenge(\phi-\psi)+2\mathchoice{\dot{u}^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{(2\phi-\psi)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;\alpha}}}}{(2\phi-\psi)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;\alpha}}}}{(2\phi-\psi)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;\alpha}}}}{(2\phi-\psi)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;\alpha}}}}+4\theta(\dot{\phi}+\dot{\psi})+6\psi\kappa(p-c_{s}^{2}\rho)-6\psi\Lambda(1+c_{s}^{2})\\
&\qquad+2(\phi+\psi)\left(2\dot{\theta}+(1+c_{s}^{2})\theta^{2}+3(1-c_{s}^{2})\sigma^{2}+(1-9c_{s}^{2})\omega^{2}\right)+2\kappa(3c_{s}^{2}-1)\,\mathchoice{q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}\mathchoice{\delta^{(1)}\!u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\delta^{(1)}\!u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\delta^{(1)}\!u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\delta^{(1)}\!u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}.\end{split}

(IV.5)

This is quite the equation to consider, so let us make some simplifying assumptions in order to increase its tractability.

1.

The perturbation is isentropic.
That is to say,
\delta S\equiv 0
. Note that this assumption is slightly stronger than assuming that the perturbation is adiabatic—see
(
3
, §2.2)
for comments on the distinction.

2.

No pure scalar contributions to stress.
Eyeing (
IV.3d
), this means
\phi=\psi
. Alternatively, this assumption can be stated as the weak-field approximation to GR that should lead to Newtonian gravity to first order. Then
\psi
(or
\phi
) represents the Newtonian potential
(
55
, §4.4)
.

3.

The equation of state is given by
p=c_{s}^{2}\rho
.
If the sound speed
c_{s}^{2}
is constant, like in epochs with component domination, then this is necessarily true. Otherwise the equation of state may vary, see
(
51
, §3.2)
.

Applying these assumptions, we arrive at what we term the
homogeneous & anisotropic, isentropic perturbation equation,
or HAIPE:

\begin{split}&\ddot{\psi}-c_{s}^{2}\lozenge\psi+\tfrac{1}{3}\mathchoice{\dot{u}^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\dot{u}^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;\alpha}}}}{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;\alpha}}}}{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;\alpha}}}}{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.8284pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.49565pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.21117pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;\alpha}}}}+\tfrac{4}{3}\theta\dot{\psi}+\left(\tfrac{4}{3}\dot{\theta}+(1+c_{s}^{2})(\tfrac{2}{3}\theta^{2}-\Lambda)+2(1-c_{s}^{2})\sigma^{2}+\tfrac{2}{3}(1-9c_{s}^{2})\omega^{2}\right)\psi\\
&\qquad=2\kappa(1-3c_{s}^{2})\,\mathchoice{q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}{q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\alpha}}}}\mathchoice{\delta^{(1)}\!u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\delta^{(1)}\!u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\delta^{(1)}\!u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\delta^{(1)}\!u^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}.\end{split}

(IV.6)

This is the equation that governs isentropic (so also adiabatic) evolutions of perturbations, in the Newtonian gauge. One notices that the rhs of this equation now depends only
\mathchoice{q^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{q^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{q^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{q^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
. Hence, if that vector vanishes (and we shall see in the next section it usually does), the rhs vanishes and we have a damped but undriven wave equation in
\psi
.

IV.2
Tensor perturbations

Gravitational waves are essentially tensor perturbations in spacetime. We can also investigate how these would travel in such anisotropic spacetimes. Concretely, thus, we assume a perturbation of the form

\mathchoice{\delta^{(1)}\!g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\delta^{(1)}\!g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\delta^{(1)}\!g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\delta^{(1)}\!g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}=2\mathchoice{E^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{E^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{E^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{E^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}},

(IV.7)

where

package for Mathematica
39
. After manual simplification, we obtain the following components of the perturbed Einstein tensor:

after

III.20
), we can thus find the following decomposed perturbation equations.

(IV.12)

As above, in circumstances where
\bm{q}\equiv 0
, the entire lhs vanishes identically. Although this equation may prove useful in some specialized circumstances, in and of itself it cannot determine the entire behavior of the perturbation (e.g. when given some initial conditions), for the reason that it is merely one equation, and
\bm{E}
has more than one degree of freedom.

V
A specific anisotropic metric choice

The result of the previous two subsections was the finding of equations (
IV.6
), (
IV.11
), and (
IV.12
). Of these, the former is the equation governing isentropic scalar perturbations, when assuming
\phi=\psi
in the perturbation (
IV.1
), and having chosen Newtonian gauge. This is thus the generalization of the Mukhanov-Sasaki perturbation equation, which is applicable only to conformally flat FLRW spacetimes with
\mathchoice{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=a^{-1}\mathchoice{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}
. In contrast, using (
IV.6
), we can investigate any spatially homogeneous spacetime, and with any fluid flow vector that we wish, so long as it has been normalized. The aim of this subsection is to calculate the terms featuring in the equations (
IV.6
), (
IV.11
), and (
IV.12
), featuring a common choice of metric components and fluid flow that nevertheless simplifies the calculations considerably.

Since we wish to consider spatially homogeneous universes, we shall choose to work in an arbitrary, i.e. generally non-coordinated, frame: as explained in Section
II.1
, this is the most natural way in which to approach this situation. Let
\bm{g}
be the metric of the spatially homogeneous spacetime we wish to investigate, and let us make the assumptions that (i) the metric, when expanded in the frame as introduced in Section
II.1
, is diagonal, and (ii) the fluid flow is
\mathchoice{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{u^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\mathchoice{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}{\delta^{{{\mu}}}_{{{0}}}}
, in that same frame. Writing

. That is, our fluid flow is geodesic in this metric, even independently of what our structure constants are. (V.11)

The term involving the structure constants in (
V.10a
) and (
V.10b
) may be interpreted as (positive resp. negative) one half of the 3-scalar curvature of the hypersurface, in the sense of the Gauss equation governing the curvature of an embedded surface.
24
. Similarly, the term involving the structure constants in (
V.10d
) is the traceless part of the 3-Ricci tensor.

The Friedmann equations

Utilizing the found components of the Einstein tensor, we can fill in the Einstein equation and find the following Friedmann equations for our cosmology.

(V.12d)

Noteworthy in these equations is that all the terms involving the structure constants have, in sum, one of their indices raised w.r.t. the definitions. This means that these contributions scale as
\propto a_{i}^{-2}
, for the appropriate scale factor
a_{i}
, so the effect/strength is similar to the influence of curvature as known from the open and closed FLRW universes. Furthermore, we note that in order to effect non-zero momentum density
\bm{q}
and anisotropic stress tensor
\bm{\pi}
, necessary conditions are (i) non-zero shear, so no identical scale factors, and (ii) non-zero structure constants, so no coordinate frame.

VI
Example: density contrasts

To assess the validity of the obtained expressions, we first investigate its results in the simple situation of a perfectly homogeneous and isotropic Universe, i.e. a conventional FLRW cosmology with a Robertson-Walker metric, and that for the anisotropic Bianchi I model. To this end, we define the mass
density contrast

\delta(x)
,

\delta(x):=\frac{\rho(x)-\overline{\rho}(t)}{\overline{\rho}(t)}\iff\rho=(1+\delta)\overline{\rho}\,.

(VI.1)

with
\rho(x)
the (energy) density at some spacetime event
x
and global energy density
\overline{\rho}(t)
given by some cosmological model
3
3

3

Note that a choice of gauge here is employed to make this relation.
. It implies the equivalent definition for
\delta:=\delta^{(1)}\!\rho/\rho
. Qualitatively
\delta>0
means that there is a local excess of energy, whereas
\delta<0
means there is a deficit, with a physical lower bound of
\delta\geq-1
.

In the situation of a FLRW cosmology, the obtained expressions should yield an evolution of the density contrast evolution that, in the early linear regime,is in accordance with the predictions of the (Newtonian) theory of perturbation growth in FLRW cosmologies (see
33
).

Knowing the forms of
\delta^{(1)}\!\rho
and
\rho
(from previous sections), on the basis of the inferred expression for the scalar perturbations (§
IV.1
) we may (i) infer the explicit expression of the density contrast, and (ii) make qualitative predictions concerning this. For the stated purposes, we consider two explicit circumstances. These are those of (i) the flat FLRW Einstein-de Sitter (EdS) case, and (ii) a Bianchi I universe. The EdS situation serves as a testbed for confirming the validity of our inferred perturbation equations. Note that our methodology
does not limit which type of Bianchi model we can analyze:
it is only for computational ease that we include Bianchi I in the present study.

VI.1
Einstein-de Sitter universe

The flat FLRW EdS universe translates to our case—in the notation of §
V
—with the following parameter choices:

\bm{C}\equiv\bm{0},\quad a_{1}(t)=a_{2}(t)=a_{3}(t)\equiv a(t),\mbox{\quad and\quad}c_{s}=0.

(VI.2)

The relations for the corresponding isotropic flow field and expansion are
\theta=3\,\dot{a}/a
and

\bm{q}=\bm{\sigma}=\bm{\pi}=\bm{0}
. This immediately yields the non-trivial Friedmann equations,

\kappa\rho=\tfrac{1}{3}\theta^{2}-\Lambda,\mbox{\quad and\quad}-2\dot{\theta}-\theta^{2}+3\Lambda=0,

(VI.3)

which implies the following expression for the evolving density perturbation
\delta^{(1)}\!\rho
and

homogeneous & anisotropic, isentropic perturbation equation,
(HAIPE)

\kappa\,\delta^{(1)}\!\rho=2\lozenge\psi-\tfrac{2}{3}\theta^{2}\psi,\mbox{\quad and\quad}3\ddot{\psi}+4\theta\dot{\psi}+[4\dot{\theta}+2\theta^{2}-3\Lambda]\psi=0\,.

(VI.4)

For an Einstein-de Sitter Universe, we may directly write the explicit dependence of expansion factor
a
and
expansion rate
\theta
on cosmic time
t
. It also involves a zero cosmological constant
\Lambda=0
. Inserting these, along with the second Friedmann equation, and simplifying the HAIPE yields

3\,\mathchoice{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[11.6019pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[11.6019pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.26111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{,00}}}}{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[11.6019pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[11.6019pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.26111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{,00}}}}{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[11.6019pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[11.6019pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.26111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{,00}}}}{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[11.6019pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[11.6019pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.26111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{,00}}}}+8t^{-1}\,\mathchoice{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.61577pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.61577pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{,0}}}}{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.61577pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.61577pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{,0}}}}{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.61577pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.61577pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{,0}}}}{\psi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.61577pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.61577pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{,0}}}}=0\implies\psi\propto t^{0}\mbox{\quad or\quad}\psi\propto t^{-5/3}.

(VI.5)

.

of

that the density contrast would evolve the same as in Newtonian perturbation theory. It provides confidence

VI.2
Bianchi I universe

Subsequently, we turn to the situation of a Bianchi I universe. We address the configuration of a
Bianchi I universe without pressure, i.e. “cosmological dust”, and without a cosmological constant, i.e.
\Lambda=0
. It involves the choice
\bm{C}\equiv\bm{0}
, while a pressureless medium, i.e.
p=0
, also implies a zero sound velocity,
c_{s}=0
. Consequently, we have
\bm{q}=\bm{0}
, and the non-trivial Friedmann equations

and\quad}\kappa\,\mathchoice{\pi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\pi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\pi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\pi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}=\mathchoice{\dot{\sigma}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\dot{\sigma}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$
